The first setting has the bar lines in the correct place. Ceolachan’s settings are set out like GHB retreat marches, moving the anacrusis to the first beat of the bar.

↳ Posted by DonaldK on April 12th, 2022.

Re: John Doherty’s

I can’t speak for Ceolachan, but he might say what you’re calling an anacrusis is not an anacrusis, but the proper first beat in the bar. It makes more sense in the B part of the tune, where almost all the bars have a strong accent on the second beat, appropriate for a mazurka.

Having said all that, it’s taken me a long time to stop tinkering with both mazurkas and pipe retreats, adding anacrusis where the cursed voice of my mis-education tells me they should be added. When I was a teenager I remember trying to “fix” a tarantella because my mind couldn’t handle the half-bar anacrusis.

In case someone is wondering, “anacrusis” is the Sunday name for pick-up notes or lead-in notes.

↳ Posted by Nigel Gatherer on April 12th, 2022.

Re: John Doherty’s

I recently found out that the reason retreats are notated with the anacrusis in the first beat of the bar is so that the tune finishes on the right foot (as all marches do, apparently).

↳ Posted by DonaldK on April 12th, 2022.

John Doherty’s, X:4 - a crooked tune

# A crooked tune
It’s a lovely tune.
The version on Bundle And Go sounded a bit crooked to me - as in, irregular bar lengths. And I find crooked tunes fascinating - so I had a go writing it down, and here’s what I came up with. I used ceolachan’s setting (#2, above) as a starting point. I think there may be a few slight inaccuracies in ceolachan’s setting; hopefully this version is an improvement.
I think having it written down may be helpful to others as there are some unusual and interesting things happening here. I find it helpful, anyway.

Also I prefer putting my full ABC here, as there’s some more info and notes in the ABC headers.
---
X: 1
T: John Doherty’s Mazurka
S: John Doherty
D: Bundle and Go
F: https://open.spotify.com/track/14llNbrqpfrhKkBB2Q94qx
N: * This is a “crooked” tune. It’s mostly in three, but there are two bars
N: in two beats, in the middle.
N: * This is just a rough approximation of Doherty’s playing. No attempt is made
N: to get his decorations, embellishments, subtleties of phrasing etc which make up such a
N: vital part of the music.
N: * Swing: sometimes two quavers are swung a bit here; and sometimes not!
N: * [A transcription](https://thesession.org/tunes/2497#setting15797) by ceolachan
N: on thesession.org was used as a starting point.
N: * The track notes for the album are shared here: https://thesession.org/recordings/344#comment756354.
N: They have this info about this mazurka:
N: “Learned from the playing of a travelling Antrim fiddler, Francie Welsch or Walsh,
N: this evocative tune is unique in the Irish tradition for its transition
N: from ¾ mazurka signature to slip jig tempo.”
N: Perhaps the “slip jig tempo” parts mentioned are the C and D sections. I would perhaps prefer
N: to use the term “hop jig tempo”.

↳ Posted by j_clark on October 26th, 2025.

Re: John Doherty’s

After digging around a bit, there appear to be some structural and melodic similarities between this tune and the version of The Green Hills of Tyrol that appears in the 1841 John Moore, Tyneside manuscript. I’m not sure if the resemblance is strong enough to suggest an actual relation or just some overlap in content, however.

↳ Posted by j_clark on November 12th, 2025.

Re: John Doherty’s

Interesting comments, j_clark. Do you have a link handy for the version of The Green Hills of Tyrol that you mentioned?

↳ Posted by GoPlayer on November 12th, 2025.

Re: John Doherty’s

Sure, a PDF is available from the Village Music Project’s page here: https://www.village-music-project.org.uk/?page_id=84.

The melodies are far from an exact match. However, after accounting for the different keys, the incipits and endings of the A parts are quite close, and they share similar descending motifs in the B part, starting on the octave, then dropping a perfect fourth, a whole step, and finally a half step (although the mazurka starts by ascending in the first measure of the B part before starting this pattern). The turnarounds at the ends of the B parts are also very thematically similar, and both lead back into a variation of the A part with some partial modulation. Again, I’m not convinced that there’s a direct relation, but I wouldn’t be surprised if there was a common source for some of the ideas.

↳ Posted by j_clark on November 12th, 2025.
